name: 酒蔵魚好人 クダコ (Sakagura Uokojin Kudako)

claims.text: As a traditional Japanese izakaya, dishes are seasoned with standard (wheat-based) soy sauce and dashi; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The kitchen centers on fish and shellfish, so vegan dishes would share preparation surfaces and fish-based dashi/soy seasoning.

claims.text: Dishes are Japanese seafood preparations (sashimi, seared fish, oysters) typically served with wheat-based soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The kitchen is centered on fish, oysters, and grilled meat, so vegan diners face pervasive cross-contact with animal ingredients.

name: 芝居茶寮 水羽 (Shibai Charyo Mizuha)

claims.text: Signature anago and oyster dishes are seasoned/glazed in the Japanese style, which uses wheat-based soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.
Core dishes (sashimi, simmered seafood, miso-based hot pots) rely on Japanese soy sauce and miso, which typically contain wheat; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
All featured dishes are seafood- and fish-dashi-based (oysters, sashimi, fish/crab hot pots); no vegan or vegetarian options are documented.

name: 新天地 みっちゃん (Shintenchi Micchan)

claims.text: The core dish is assembled on a shared iron griddle from a wheat-flour batter and wheat noodles; flour and gluten are pervasive throughout the cooking surface, so cross-contamination is unavoidable for a gluten-sensitive diner.
Okonomiyaki is finished with a standard wheat-based okonomiyaki sauce (not gluten-free).
Pork, egg, squid/shrimp and bonito-style toppings are standard on the shared griddle, so vegan cross-contact is unavoidable.
Shabu-shabu and hot pot are served with ponzu and miso-based sauces/broths, which are typically wheat-containing soy seasonings.
The kitchen is built around boar and game meat with meat/fish-based hot pot broths, so even tofu and vegetable dishes share a thoroughly non-vegan cooking environment.
